title: Hilsa output down 10% in three years, Dhaka workshop hears
excerpt: Bangladesh's hilsa catch has fallen about 10% since a record 571,000 tonnes in FY2022-23, experts said at a Bay of Bengal workshop in Dhaka, TBS reports.

image.alt: Hilsa fish piled in a basket at Karwan Bazar market in Dhaka

content:
DHAKA, 28 November 2026: Bangladesh's hilsa production has fallen by about 10% over the past three fiscal years after a decade of growth, a researcher told a regional workshop in Dhaka on Friday (27 November), The Business Standard (TBS) reported.

Output rose from 351,000 tonnes in 2012-13 to a record 571,000 tonnes in FY2022-23, according to a presentation by hilsa researcher Mohammad Anisur Rahman, before declining. He named overfishing, illegal fishing, banned nets, silting and new chars in hilsa habitats, water pollution and warmer water linked to climate change as the main causes, TBS said. Bangladesh accounts for more than 80% of global hilsa production, and the fish generates more than $3 billion a year in harvesting and trade across the region, according to the report.

The three-day workshop, Sustainable Management of Hilsa Fisheries in the Bay of Bengal Region, brings together officials and researchers from Bangladesh, India and Myanmar. Agriculture, Fisheries and Livestock Minister Mohammed Aminur Rashid, who opened it, called the decline a matter of concern and said the government would not tolerate overfishing or banned nets. He said natural factors such as underwater silting and climate change were also to blame, and called for science-based management and regional cooperation.

The minister highlighted the debts of small-scale fishers, many of whom borrow at high interest from informal lenders known as dadondars, and called for easier access to affordable institutional loans and microcredit, TBS reported. Indian researcher Amiya Sahu proposed a regional hilsa database and task force. Kin Maung Soe, former head of WorldFish in Myanmar, said production was also falling there. Workshop convener Abdul Wahab said the decline was "not irreversible" if science-based management and regional cooperation were ensured.

The workshop is organised by the Bay of Bengal Programme Inter-Governmental Organisation (BOBP-IGO), Bangladesh Maritime University, Noakhali Science and Technology University, Bangladesh Agricultural University and WorldFish.

Why it matters

Hilsa supports fishers, boat workers, processors and traders along the coast and the big rivers, many of them poor and in debt. Lower catches cut incomes and can push families towards more borrowing or migration. Food assistance during fishing bans is only part of the answer if the fish keeps declining. Devlens has reported on coastal fishers demanding climate grants, not loans and on how silting rivers are cutting off char communities.

What to watch

  • Recommendations from the workshop when it closes on Sunday (29 November), including any regional database or task force.
  • Department of Fisheries production figures for FY2025-26.
  • Whether fishers get cheaper credit, as the minister proposed.

Sources
